What to check before using Keyword Eye

Start with a service and one geographic market. Separate searches for how to solve the problem from searches for a provider, then match each group to the most helpful page.

Build a keyword list

Choose a service and one geographic market. Write down the language customers use in enquiries. Look for specific variations that describe the service rather than unrelated topics.

Use a small plumbing company choosing pages for different services as the test case. The project starts with customer enquiry phrases, live search results, and service area information. Write down where each item came from and when you checked it. Keep the material together so the person reviewing the outcome can see what the first decision was based on. Agree on one definition of a successful result before starting. In this case, the project is ready to move ahead when each query group points to a page that serves the visitor.

Consider how the task changes for emergency callers and planned repair customers. Each audience may have a different first question. Write those questions in ordinary language, using wording you would expect to hear from a real person. Choose one audience for the first pass. That gives you a sensible reason to put one piece of information first and leave the rest for later.

Keep the boundaries of the trial visible. Write what is included, what you will record and what you will check independently. A clear boundary also makes it easier to explain why you excluded queries for jobs outside the actual service area. Put exclusions next to the decision they affected. If the boundary turns out to be too narrow, adjust it before comparing the results and write down what changed.

Prepare a starting example that has enough detail to expose a real problem. Use ordinary input you can share with a reviewer. Keep a copy of the original alongside the working version. A colleague should be able to compare them and point to the exact difference. When someone wants to reproduce the exercise, give them the same inputs and record whether they reached the same initial decision.

The first handoff should include your question, the inputs and the expected result. Choose a suitable format for the project. For local plumbing keywords, a small table or a short written brief is often enough. Before starting the next step, make sure each item is traceable. A reviewer should be able to see who supplied it, whether it is current and how its accuracy affects the eventual decision.

Group search intent

Group terms into learning, comparing and ready-to-buy queries. Inspect search results for each group to see what sort of page people expect.

Use the information you prepared to produce two comparable examples. Keep the goal and audience stable while you change one meaningful detail. Record that detail in a sentence before running the comparison. Afterward, note what you observed and which part of the output changed. If the input itself has changed, record it separately and start a clean comparison.

The output at this stage should make the path toward a keyword-to-page map clearer. Ask a colleague to review one complete example. Give them the original materials and have them explain the connection between those materials and the result. If the reviewer has to guess why you made a choice, add a short evidence note before asking them to judge the quality.

Look for a point where a plausible result could lead you in the wrong direction. In this workflow that could be queries for jobs outside the actual service area. Think through what would happen if that slipped into the final decision. Then check the closest underlying source and replace the unsupported assumption. If you cannot resolve the question during the trial, record it as an open decision with a clear owner.

For a version aimed at property managers, check whether the wording, detail or format needs to change. Carry over the facts that apply to both versions. Record any change that depends on the audience so an editor can distinguish a deliberate adjustment from a mistake. The second version can expose assumptions that seemed harmless in the first.

At this point, compare your sample with the work you already do. Time the parts that need another review and note what still has to happen outside Keyword Eye. A fast first result can lead to additional verification or revision. Include that time when you evaluate whether the workflow improves delivery. If a limitation makes manual review necessary, make room for it in the project plan.

Choose target pages

Match each query group to an existing or planned page. Use Search Console after publication to see whether the intended page earns impressions for the relevant terms.

Before handoff, open the starting materials and the proposed final result together. Check the part of the job that has the greatest effect on the intended audience. Use this acceptance condition: each query group points to a page that serves the visitor. Note which sources support that judgment and who has the authority to approve it. Save the resulting a keyword-to-page map with the project files.

Check the output in the setting where it will be used. In the case of local plumbing keywords, think about the person who will see it without the background you have. Give them enough context to understand the purpose and next action. If they need to open a separate file to interpret a basic term or find its source, update the handoff notes.

Choose what would trigger a second review. Examples include a new workspace, a different data source or a change to the buyer offer. Write the trigger beside the decision it affects. When you return to the project, you can review that particular detail before redoing everything. The same record helps you identify the date at which an old result stopped being reliable.

If you plan to repeat the task, preserve a clean sample from this trial. Include an example input, the accepted result and the reasons that led you to accept it. Add one example of a problem you would reject, such as queries for jobs outside the actual service area. A future reviewer can use these examples to assess a new result without guessing what the first team meant.

Record the final status in straightforward terms. List what you verified, what you left open and what action follows. If the next action belongs to someone else, tell them which workspace or files to use and when the work should be checked. For shared accounts, keep copies of deliverables you need later and understand who can access the working material.

Worked example: Local plumbing keywords

Consider a small plumbing company choosing pages for different services. Define the decision before opening any tool. One person prepares customer enquiry phrases, live search results, and service area information, while another reviews whether the materials match the intended work. If the examples in the sample concern different products, readers or dates, narrow the project until the team can explain why the remaining cases belong together.

Run a small version from start to finish. Begin with the first task described above, keep the same inputs for the next task, and save a dated copy at every handoff. This makes it possible to trace a disagreement back to the supporting fact or chosen setting. In a shared workspace, keep the review copy somewhere the rest of your team can access independently.

For this exercise, the main warning sign is queries for jobs outside the actual service area. Decide how you will spot it before approving the work. Keep a reference copy and ask the reviewer to mark where the problem would show up. The exercise is successful when each query group points to a page that serves the visitor. A successful small trial gives you useful evidence for this specific workflow. A larger project may require a separate test when the audience, volume or access terms change.

Now review the result with someone who represents the next person in the chain. If reviewers include emergency callers and property managers, give them the same basic material and ask the same opening question. Listen for a difference in what they notice or how they interpret the result. Document that difference before deciding whether a single version can serve both groups.

Finish by creating a keyword-to-page map. Include a date, the source materials and a short explanation of the decision. If you have an open issue, write what would resolve it. A test involving an unknown account feature can often be closed with a live demonstration using harmless sample material. A question about rights or access terms needs the applicable documentation or a written response from the provider.

Decide whether the offer fits your work

Begin with the part of the workflow that matters most. Do you need the same user, source data, stored projects or export settings over several weeks? Ask the provider to show the exact workspace and walk through your highest-priority task. Keep the discussion specific. For this product, the sample scenario and criteria above give you a practical way to describe the task.

Compare the access period with your real project schedule. If the work needs to be reviewed next month, check whether the source material and output will still be available. If you can use a sample without connecting a production website, store, account or customer file, start there. Confirm which steps require additional permissions or a separate subscription before moving a team onto the service.

When reviewing pricing, use the amount and billing conditions shown at checkout. Take into account setup and review time. The useful comparison is the cost of completing the work to the standard you need. A less expensive offer may need more manual coordination. A direct plan may have options that matter for a recurring team project. Ask which features apply to the specific workspace before making the comparison.

Review checklist

  • The intended user and project outcome are written down.
  • Your sample is representative and appropriate for the workspace.
  • You saved an original copy and documented the inputs.
  • The reviewer looked at queries for jobs outside the actual service area.
  • The result meets the condition that each query group points to a page that serves the visitor.
  • The handoff includes a keyword-to-page map, the review date and any remaining questions.

Comparing access options

Check the subscription duration and current features on the SEOGBTools listing. Compare the offer against the vendor’s own account options if you need a private workspace, saved projects or particular export formats. The SEOGBTools shop lists related products.

Frequently asked questions

What should I test first with Keyword Eye?

Choose a service and one geographic market. Write down the language customers use in enquiries. Look for specific variations that describe the service rather than unrelated topics.

Where can I confirm usage limits?

Confirm the exact current product, workspace and limits through live chat before ordering.

How do I compare two access options?

Use the same example for both. Write down the intended result, the time available for review and any export or permissions required. If one option provides a demo, check that it is the same product and version you would receive. Include manual steps and the time needed to complete them when you decide which plan fits.

What should I record before I repeat the workflow?

Keep a dated version of the inputs and the accepted result. Include the account or workspace version if it affects the outcome. Add a sentence describing what would justify rechecking the work. For local plumbing keywords, use the evidence you collected to show why the final decision was made.

What if the test output differs from what I expected?

Check whether the example, account or settings changed. Review your source records to see whether the original expectation was supported. Use the smallest correction that addresses the issue and repeat the test under the same conditions. If you still cannot explain the difference, ask the provider about the specific step or feature that failed.

Can I use a shared workspace for ongoing client work?

Confirm who can access saved projects, whether data can be exported and whether you can retrieve the finished material after the access period. Use public or approved sample inputs for an initial trial. If the project involves private client documents or advertising accounts, follow the client’s access requirements and use an arrangement that supports them.
